title: You See, But You Do Not Observe
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from "A Scandal in Bohemia," in The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes by Arthur Conan Doyle (1892).
body: "It is simplicity itself," said he; "my eyes tell me that on the inside of your left shoe, just where the firelight strikes it, the leather is scored by six almost parallel cuts. Obviously they have been caused by someone who has very carelessly scraped round the edges of the sole in order to remove crusted mud from it. Hence, you see, my double deduction that you had been out in vile weather, and that you had a particularly malignant boot-slitting specimen of the London slavey."

I could not help laughing at the ease with which he explained his process of deduction. "When I hear you give your reasons," I remarked, "the thing always appears to me to be so ridiculously simple that I could easily do it myself, though at each successive instance of your reasoning I am baffled until you explain your process. And yet I believe that my eyes are as good as yours." "Quite so," he answered, lighting a cigarette, and throwing himself down into an armchair. "You see, but you do not observe. The distinction is clear."

"For example, you have frequently seen the steps which lead up from the hall to this room." "Frequently." "How often?" "Well, some hundreds of times." "Then how many are there?" "How many? I don't know." "Quite so! You have not observed. And yet you have seen. That is just my point. Now, I know that there are seventeen steps, because I have both seen and observed."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Holmes say caused the six almost parallel cuts on Watson's shoe?
options: Someone carelessly scraping round the edges of the sole to remove crusted mud
Watson kicking a stone on his walk
A tear from walking through thick brush
Watson's dog chewing on the leather

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what "double deduction" does Holmes make from examining the shoe?
options: That Watson had been out in vile weather and had a careless, boot-slitting servant girl
That Watson had traveled abroad recently and lost weight
That Watson had taken up a new hobby and injured his foot
That Watson had visited a shoemaker and bought new boots

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does Watson describe Holmes's explanations once they are given?
options: Ridiculously simple, though baffling before they were explained
Impossible to follow even after explanation
Obvious from the very first moment
Too technical for him to understand at all

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what does Holmes do as he answers "Quite so"?
options: He lights a cigarette and throws himself down into an armchair
He stands up and paces the room
He picks up a magnifying glass
He pours himself a glass of water

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how many times has Watson seen the steps leading up to the room?
options: Some hundreds of times
Only once
About a dozen times
He has never seen them before

questions.prompt: Per the passage, how many steps does Holmes say lead up from the hall?
options: Seventeen
Twelve
Twenty
Seven

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Holmes say, "You see, but you do not observe"?
options: He means that merely looking at something differs from consciously noting and analyzing its details
He means that Watson's eyesight is physically weaker than his own
He means that Watson refuses to look at anything closely
He means that Watson has never actually visited the room before

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Holmes bring up the number of steps right after Watson claims his eyes are as good as Holmes's?
options: To demonstrate concretely that good eyesight alone does not equal true observation
To change the subject away from his deduction about the shoe
To test whether Watson can count quickly under pressure
To prove that the house has been recently renovated

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: Holmes demonstrates that careful, deliberate observation reveals far more than simply seeing, using both the shoe and the staircase as proof
Holmes admits that his deductions are often just lucky guesses
Watson proves that he observes details just as well as Holmes does
The passage shows that Holmes and Watson disagree about the weather

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does Holmes mean by "observe"?
options: To consciously notice and register details, not just look at something
To politely comment on something out loud
To obey a rule or instruction
To celebrate a special occasion

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where on Watson's shoe did Holmes notice the scored cuts?
options: On the inside of the left shoe, where the firelight strikes it
On the toe of the right shoe
On the heel of both shoes
On the laces of the left shoe

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what does Watson say he could do once Holmes explains his reasoning?
options: Easily do it himself
Never understand it at all
Explain it better than Holmes
Prove Holmes wrong

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Watson believe about his own eyes compared to Holmes's?
options: That his eyes are just as good as Holmes's
That his eyes are far better than Holmes's
That his eyes are much weaker than Holmes's
That his eyes have never been tested

questions.prompt: Per the passage, how does Holmes say he knows there are seventeen steps?
options: Because he has both seen and observed them
Because he counted them once, long ago
Because a builder told him the exact number
Because he measured the staircase with a tape

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Holmes's explanation about the shoe and the servant girl seem convincing to Watson despite being unusual?
options: Holmes lays out a clear, step-by-step chain of physical evidence connecting each detail to its cause
Watson has seen the servant girl misbehave many times before
Holmes had already met the servant girl in person
Watson had already guessed the same explanation himself

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what the exchange about the staircase teaches?
options: Seeing something many times is not the same as truly observing and remembering its details
Watson has a poor memory compared to most people
Holmes has never actually walked up the staircase himself
The number of steps in a house rarely matters to anyone

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that Watson had been out in "vile" weather?
options: Extremely unpleasant or bad weather
Unusually warm and sunny weather
Weather typical for springtime
Weather that had been predicted in advance
